summary: Controlled study of 'tool architecture' in coding agents: six capability-matched tool setups (BashOnly, Atomic file tools, NLSearch subagent, Python CodeAct, HypoTrack, Scratchpad) on a 65-instance SWE-bench Live subset with three actors and 10 rollouts each (11,700 trajectories). Resolve rates are broadly unchanged, but Atomic tools raise pass^k consistency, NLSearch broadens file exploration, Python code-as-action cuts steps and input tokens, and lightweight thinking tools do little.

claims.claim: Structured low-level (Atomic) tools improve repeated-attempt consistency by up to 4.7x, for all three actors.
claims.evidence: Table 2: Qwen3Coder-30B pass^9 0.020 -> 0.094 (the 4.7x is a ratio on a near-zero base); Kimi-K2.5 +0.013-0.014 and Sonnet-4.5 +0.017-0.031 absolute. Direction consistent; Appendix B.2 repeats Bash vs Atomic with 3x more attempts for open-weight actors. No CIs/significance.

claims.claim: Python CodeAct-style interface matches task performance with 41.6% fewer steps and 56.3% lower token usage.
claims.evidence: Exact 41.6%/56.3% figures not found in body text; Table 8 shows step reductions 77->46, 65->47, 80->55 (~28-40%); input tokens shown only in Figure 4. Direction supported, headline magnitudes not traceable in the extracted text. Resolve-rate parity shown only as Figure 5 without numbers.

claims.claim: Natural-language search broadens exploration and increases access to relevant files by >11%, with lower precision.
claims.evidence: Figure 3 read-diversity deltas; Table 7 recall/precision vs a high-relevant-file proxy, which is validated on 30 trajectories / 619 file ops at 94.4% precision, 97.6% recall (LLM-assisted human labels). NLSearch is a same-model subagent using grep, so its subagent token cost is a confound for efficiency.

claims.claim: Lightweight cognitive-scaffolding tools (scratchpad, hypothesis tracking) have limited effect.
claims.evidence: Table 2 mixed/negative deltas for Scratchpad and HypoTrack; Appendix C qualitative analysis that actors restate existing reasoning. Authors scope claim to lightweight scaffolds.

patterns.note: Python code-as-action reduces interaction steps and cumulative input tokens at similar resolve rate across three actors (Table 8).
Grep/bash baseline is competitive on resolve rate; NL search over grep raises recall but lowers precision.
NLSearch is implemented as a same-model exploration subagent: broader exploration, not more diverse solutions or higher resolve rate.
Shows that how a small tool set is exposed changes behavior even at fixed capability; does not study catalog size.
Interface choice is a cost lever: fewer steps -> lower cumulative input tokens.
SWE-bench Live subset main eval; SWE-bench Verified/Pro and a debugging split as generalization checks (two open-weight actors, 5 rollouts).

methodology.sample: 65 SWE-bench Live instances (25 of 100 repos sampled, <=5 issues each); 10 rollouts x 6 setups x 3 actors = 11,700 trajectories; extra study on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, debugging split with 5 rollouts.
methodology.baselines: BashOnly (mini-swe-agent-style) as reference; all setups built by the authors to be capability-matched.
methodology.models: Qwen3Coder-30B, Kimi-K2.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (generalization study: only the two open-weight models).
methodology.variance: Repeated rollouts used to compute pass^k; no confidence intervals or significance tests reported.
methodology.ablations: The six setups are themselves the ablation; mechanism analyses in Appendix B.3-B.5.
methodology.contamination_controls: SWE-bench Live chosen as contamination-controlled benchmark.
methodology.languages: SWE-bench Live repos (predominantly Python); no Java evaluation.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; acknowledgments thank anonymous reviewers but no venue stated

biases.detail: 'Up to 4.7x' consistency is a ratio of 0.094 to 0.020 for the weakest model; for strong actors the gain is 1-3 absolute points.
Ten rollouts give pass^k but no CIs/significance on deltas as small as 0.013.
SWE-bench Live/Verified/Pro subsets; no Java or statically typed repo results.
65 instances from 25 repos in the main study.
Headline 41.6% steps / 56.3% tokens not traceable to a body table; Table 8 shows 28-40% step reductions.
NLSearch subagent cost accounting not clearly separated; efficiency comparison may understate NLSearch cost.

coi.affiliations: Purdue University, Microsoft Research, University of Chicago; first author interned at Microsoft Research.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: No Microsoft product evaluated; actors are Qwen, Kimi, Anthropic models; tool setups are generic.
coi.funding: Microsoft Internship Program, NSF, DARPA, ONR.
coi.detail: Vendor-affiliated co-authors, but no self-promotion of a vendor product.

verdict_reason: Well-controlled capability-matched design with many repeated rollouts and released code, but Python-only tasks, no significance testing, inflated ratio headline, and the token/step headline numbers are not traceable to body tables.
applicability: Directly informs tool design for the team's harness, regardless of host: (1) give agents a small set of structured edit/view/search primitives rather than bash alone to improve run-to-run consistency, which matters for repeatable ingestion jobs; (2) allow a code-execution action (in a Java shop this could be a JShell/Groovy/script step or a CLI wrapper) to cut steps and token cost; (3) scratchpad/'think' tools add little and can be dropped from the catalog. Caveats: evidence is Python repos only, single-repo tasks, so effects on a Maven/Gradle multi-module Java codebase spanning 4+ repos are unmeasured; and mixed hosts (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex) fix their own tool architecture, so the team can only influence this via MCP/CLI tools it exposes.

conflicts_with.detail: Both find grep/bash baselines hard to beat on outcomes; LSP study shows semantic tools add tokens, consistent with NLSearch raising recall but lowering precision here.
